subject: History
description: Covers Iltutmish, Alauddin Khilji market reforms, and Tughlaq capital shift.

questions.stem: Who is generally considered the real founder of the Delhi Sultanate, having shifted the capital from Lahore to Delhi and saving it from Mongol invasions?

options.option_text: Iltutmish
Qutb-ud-din Aibak
Razia Sultana
Balban

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: While Qutb-ud-din Aibak founded the Mamluk (Slave) dynasty, he ruled from Lahore and his reign was very short (4 years). It was his son-in-law, Shams-ud-din Iltutmish, who shifted the capital to Delhi, organized the administration, introduced the standard silver coin (Tanka) and copper coin (Jital), and diplomatically saved India from the wrath of Genghis Khan by refusing asylum to a fleeing Central Asian prince. Therefore, historians call him the real founder.
DECOY BUSTING: Aibak was the first ruler but not the consolidator. Razia was Iltutmish's daughter (the only female ruler). Balban was a later Mamluk ruler known for his iron-fisted "blood and iron" policy.
EXAM INSIGHT: Iltutmish also created the 'Turkan-i-Chahalgani' (The Group of Forty), an elite corps of Turkish nobles who held immense power, which Balban later brutally destroyed to centralize his own authority.

questions.stem: Which Sultan of Delhi implemented strict market control and price regulation policies to maintain a massive standing army without bankrupting the state treasury?

options.option_text: Alauddin Khilji
Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Firoz Shah Tughlaq
Sikandar Lodi

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Alauddin Khilji maintained the largest standing army of the Delhi Sultanate to defend against Mongol invasions and to fund his rapid conquests of South India. To pay this massive army without draining the treasury, he fixed the prices of all essential commodities (grains, cloth, horses, slaves) at artificially low rates in Delhi. He appointed strict market controllers (Shahna-i-Mandi) and spies (Munhiyans) to ensure merchants didn't hoard or overcharge.
DECOY BUSTING: Muhammad bin Tughlaq is famous for his disastrous experiments (shifting capital to Daulatabad, token currency). Firoz Shah Tughlaq built many canals and cities. Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra.
EXAM INSIGHT: Alauddin was also the first Sultan to pay his soldiers entirely in cash (rather than land grants/iqtas) and introduced the branding of horses (Dagh) and maintaining a descriptive roll of soldiers (Huliya) to prevent corruption in the army.

questions.stem: The ambitious but disastrous decision to shift the capital of the Sultanate from Delhi to Devagiri (renamed Daulatabad) in the Deccan was taken by:

options.option_text: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Alauddin Khilji
Balban
Ibrahim Lodi

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (often called the 'Mad Sultan' or a visionary ahead of his time) shifted his capital to Daulatabad (in modern Maharashtra) in 1327. He reasoned that Daulatabad was centrally located and would allow him to control the newly conquered South Indian territories while being safe from Mongol invasions in the North. However, he ordered the entire population of Delhi to march 1,500 km south, leading to immense suffering and death.
DECOY BUSTING: Alauddin Khilji conquered the Deccan but ruled from Delhi. Balban never crossed the Vindhyas. Ibrahim Lodi was the last Sultan, defeated by Babur.
EXAM INSIGHT: Realizing his mistake when he couldn't control rebellions in the North from the South, Tughlaq ordered everyone back to Delhi a few years later. His other famous failed experiment was introducing 'Token Currency' (copper/brass coins meant to have the value of silver), which led to massive counterfeiting in every household.

questions.stem: The 'Iqta' system, widely used throughout the Delhi Sultanate, was essentially an assignment of ?

options.option_text: Revenue from a territory granted to nobles in lieu of cash salary
Hereditary land ownership rights given to military commanders permanently
A tax collected from trade guilds and merchants by the Sultan's agents
Agricultural loans extended by the crown to landless cultivators

questions.explanation: An Iqta was the assignment of the revenue of a particular territory to a noble or military officer (Iqtadar) in lieu of cash salary — the holder administered the area and kept revenues after paying troops. It was NOT hereditary ownership (Option B), which is the commonest misconception; ownership of land remained with the state.

questions.stem: Razia Sultana, the only woman to sit on the throne of the Delhi Sultanate, was the daughter and specifically nominated successor of which Sultan?

options.option_text: Qutb-ud-din Aibak, founder of the Mamluk dynasty in 1206 CE
Iltutmish, the third Sultan who formally organised the Sultanate
Balban, the powerful and authoritarian ninth Sultan of Delhi
Nasiruddin Mahmud, the pious eighth Sultan who ruled alongside Balban

questions.explanation: Iltutmish publicly nominated Razia as his successor — a highly unusual step — recognising her ability over his sons. Option A is wrong because Aibak died in 1210 and Razia came to power in 1236; Option C (Balban) is a common confusion since Balban dominated the later Sultanate but Razia pre-dates him as ruler.

questions.stem: The 'Chahalgani' or 'Corps of Forty', a clique of powerful Turkish nobles who controlled key governorships and posts, was decisively broken by which Delhi Sultan?

options.option_text: Razia Sultana, who tried to sideline them by promoting non-Turkish nobles
Iltutmish, who had originally created this group to consolidate power
Balban, who used systematic terror and elimination to crush their influence
Alauddin Khalji, who neutralised nobles through his market-control system

questions.explanation: Ghiyasuddin Balban (r. 1266–1287) systematically destroyed the Chahalgani through banishments, executions, and confiscation of iqtas, centralising power in the Sultan. Razia (Option A) challenged them but was overthrown by the same nobles. Iltutmish (Option B) formed the group, not disbanded it. Alauddin (Option D) is chronologically later and his market reforms targeted merchants, not this noble corps.

questions.stem: The Alai Darwaza, completed in 1311 CE and celebrated as a landmark of early Indo-Islamic architecture for its true dome and red sandstone with white marble inlay, was built as the southern gateway to which structure?

options.option_text: Siri Fort, the second city of Delhi founded by Alauddin Khalji himself
Hauz Khas reservoir complex commissioned to supply water to Siri city
Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque within the Qutb Minar complex at Mehrauli
Tughlaqabad Fort constructed later by Ghiyasuddin Tughluq in 1321 CE

questions.explanation: Alauddin Khalji built the Alai Darwaza as the southern entrance gateway to the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (the first mosque built in Delhi by Qutb-ud-din Aibak). It is noted for employing a true semicircular dome — a first in the subcontinent. Siri Fort (Option A) and Tughlaqabad (Option D) are separate fortified cities with no connection to this gateway.

questions.stem: In the Delhi Sultanate's central administration, the department headed by the 'Ariz-i-Mamalik' was called Diwan-i-Arz. What was its primary responsibility?

options.option_text: Assessing and collecting land revenue across all provinces of the Sultanate
Maintaining army muster rolls, inspecting soldiers, and supervising horse quality
Drafting royal farmans and managing the Sultan's official correspondence
Hearing appeals against provincial judgments as the court of second instance

questions.explanation: The Diwan-i-Arz was the military department; the Ariz-i-Mamalik maintained descriptive rolls (chehra) of soldiers and inspected army contingents and horses — later formalised by Alauddin Khalji. Revenue was handled by the Diwan-i-Wizarat (Option A), correspondence by the Diwan-i-Insha (Option C), and appeals by the Diwan-i-Mazalim (Option D).

questions.stem: Alauddin Khalji introduced two specific military-administrative measures to prevent soldiers from presenting borrowed or inferior horses during musters and inflating troop numbers. What were these measures called?

options.option_text: Iqta and Khiraj — land-assignment and land-revenue taxation for army funding
Dagh (branding of horses) and Chehra (descriptive roll of each soldier)
Tanka and Jital — silver and copper coin denominations fixed for army pay
Mansab and Jagir — rank-assignment and revenue-grant system for officers

questions.explanation: Alauddin Khalji introduced the Dagh system (royal brand on horses to prevent substitution) and Chehra (physical description register of each soldier) to curb fraudulent musters. Option D (Mansab-Jagir) is a common trap — that system belongs to the Mughal Empire, not the Delhi Sultanate. Tanka/Jital (Option C) refers to currency, not military registers.

questions.stem: The Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451 CE) that ruled Delhi after Timur's devastating invasion derived its political legitimacy by acknowledging the suzerainty of which external ruler?

options.option_text: Shahrukh, son of Timur and Timurid ruler of Samarkand and Khorasan
Muzaffar Shah I of Gujarat, who declared independence after Timur's raid
Husain Shah Sharqi of Jaunpur, the rival eastern power bordering Delhi
Bahlul Khan Lodi, the Afghan noble who later replaced the Sayyid rulers

questions.explanation: Khizr Khan, founder of the Sayyid dynasty, had been Timur's governor of the Punjab. He and his successors read the khutba (Friday sermon) in the name of Shahrukh — Timur's son and Timurid heir — to legitimise their rule, never claiming independent sovereign status. Option D (Bahlul Lodi) is the dynasty that replaced the Sayyids in 1451, not a suzerain; Gujarat (B) and Jaunpur (C) were rival regional powers, not overlords.
